analysis.one_liner: Insures up to $10 million in noninterest-bearing business checking accounts at banks other than the largest.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing in February 2026 on a bipartisan bill to insure up to $10 million of business transaction accounts, but it has not received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails, the FDIC guarantees each depositor only up to a standard limit. This bill would add a separate guarantee of up to $10 million for checking accounts that pay no interest — the accounts businesses, nonprofits, and local governments use for payroll and operating expenses. The coverage would apply at banks and credit unions, but not at the subsidiaries of the biggest global systemically important banks or foreign bank branches. New premiums to fund the coverage would phase in over ten years, and banks with $10 billion or less in assets would be exempt from special assessments during that period.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, nonprofits, and local governments holding large noninterest-bearing transaction accounts would keep access to payroll and operating funds even if their bank fails, instead of losing everything above the standard insurance limit. Community and regional banks would gain, because large transaction depositors would have a reason to keep those deposits at banks that can offer the coverage — which excludes the largest banks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses, nonprofits, and community banks

how_it_helps.text: The FDIC would insure the net amount, up to $10 million per depositor, held in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts at insured banks, with deposits across subsidiaries of one holding company counted together against the limit.
Credit unions would get parallel coverage: the NCUA would insure up to $10 million in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts per member.

The coverage excludes subsidiaries of global systemically important bank holding companies and insured branches of foreign banks, steering the insured large-balance business away from the biggest institutions.

During a ten-year transition, the FDIC would publish a plan for gradually folding the new coverage into its assessment base, and banks with total assets of $10 billion or less would not have to pay special assessments tied to the new coverage.

analysis.who_pays: The FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund — funded by bank premiums and backed ultimately by taxpayers — would absorb added loss risk on accounts it now insures for free of the standard limit, and full premiums would not apply for ten years. Banks above the $10 billion asset threshold would pay higher assessments during the phase-in, costs that banks generally pass along to customers. Insuring large business balances also makes it easier for banks to rely on big, flighty deposits without paying the full price of that risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: FDIC insurance fund and mid-size banks' customers

drawbacks.text: The bill extends insurance to large balances while delaying the premiums that would fund it: banks with $10 billion or less in assets pay no special assessments for the new coverage during the ten-year transition, shifting the cost of the added risk onto the insurance fund and the banks that do pay.

Blanket insurance on large transaction accounts reduces the discipline that large uninsured depositors normally impose on banks; if big operating deposits are fully protected, depositors have less reason to prefer well-managed banks, and losses in a failure fall on the fund rather than on the large depositors.

The $10 million coverage applies only to accounts that pay no interest, so the benefit goes to entities that keep large operating balances — businesses, nonprofits, governments — rather than to typical household savers, and the exclusion of the largest banks means coverage depends on where a business banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea has real value: in the 2023 regional bank failures, operating accounts holding payrolls froze above the insurance limit, and guaranteeing those accounts would protect workers' paychecks and local governments from a bank collapse they did nothing to cause. But the design carries a genuine cost: it socializes the risk of large business deposits through the insurance fund while letting small banks defer the premiums for a decade, and it dulls the market pressure that uninsured deposits put on bank management. A well-built version would pair the coverage with full, immediate risk-based premiums.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in October 2025, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and the committee held a hearing on it in February 2026; no markup or floor vote has happened and the Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Hagerty introduced the Main Street Depositor Protection Act on October 9, 2025, joined by Sen. Angela Alsobrooks as cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the day it was introduced.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on February 5, 2026 — the only committee action recorded since referral.

The bill text would amend the Federal Deposit Insurance Act to insure up to $10 million per depositor in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts, exclude subsidiaries of global systemically important bank holding companies and foreign bank branches, and extend parallel coverage to credit unions.

During a ten-year transition, the FDIC and NCUA would publish plans to phase the new coverage into their assessment bases, and banks with $10 billion or less in assets would be exempt from special assessments tied to the new coverage.
No vote has been scheduled in the Senate or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet: nothing has changed, so large transaction depositors remain insured only up to the standard limit and the insurance fund's exposure is unchanged. If the bill dies in committee, the status quo continues — which leaves payroll-account risk with businesses and leaves the assessment holiday that small banks would have received off the table.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill awaits committee action

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend FDIC insurance to $10 million for noninterest-bearing transaction accounts.

for.name: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from introduction.

for.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
for.what_they_did: Received the referral and held a hearing on the bill on February 5, 2026; has not scheduled a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no recorded opposition or vote has occurred yet.

industries.note: These banks could offer $10 million coverage on large business transaction accounts, attracting deposits that would otherwise sit with the biggest banks — and banks with $10 billion or less in assets pay no special assessments for the new coverage during the ten-year transition. The coverage does protect their small-business depositors, but the deferred premiums shift the cost of the added risk onto the insurance fund.

Subsidiaries of the largest globally systemically important bank holding companies are barred from offering the new coverage, so large transaction depositors have an incentive to move operating funds to smaller banks. Their loss is a competitive one rather than a direct public cost.

Credit unions get parallel authority to insure up to $10 million in members' noninterest-bearing transaction accounts, with the NCUA board authorized to regulate to keep the share insurance fund well-capitalized.

industries.industry: FDIC Deposit Insurance Fund (banking industry assessment base and its taxpayer backstop)
industries.note: The fund takes on loss exposure on accounts up to $10 million without full premiums for ten years, and the fund is ultimately backstopped by taxpayers. That added tail risk is borne by the system rather than by the large depositors who benefit.

analysis.trajectory: With one hearing and a single bipartisan cosponsor, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee unless the Banking Committee schedules a markup; standalone deposit-insurance bills rarely reach the floor on their own. The most plausible advance would be attachment to a broader banking or financial-regulation package, especially if regional-bank stability resurfaces as a live concern.
